notes: Teacher strike pay deduction; Burgundy Book incorporation and statutory pay scheme interaction are clearly resolved.

enrichment.short_title: Teacher strike salary deduction under Burgundy Book

statutes_considered.title: School Teachers Pay and Conditions Act 1991
School Teachers' Pay and Conditions Document 2001

key_facts: A Kent County Council teacher participated in a one-day strike on 14 March 2002 and had £113 deducted, calculated as 1/195th of her annual salary.
Her contract incorporated the Burgundy Book, which clause 3.2 provides strike deductions at 1/365th of annual salary.
The council argued the statutory School Teachers' Pay and Conditions Document, with its 195-day working year, displaced the Burgundy Book provision.
Similar cases affecting other teachers turned on the same principles.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Claim for a declaration as to the lawful amount of salary deduction following strike action.
enrichment.outcome: Claimant succeeded; declaration granted that the maximum lawful deduction was 1/365th of annual salary, not 1/195th.
enrichment.ratio: Clause 3.2 of the Burgundy Book was incorporated into the teacher's contract and was not inconsistent with the statutory pay and working-time scheme; the statutory document sets core remuneration and working time but does not exclude collective agreement on strike deductions.
legal_issues: Whether Burgundy Book clause 3.2 was incorporated into the contract
Whether clause 3.2 was inconsistent with the 2001 Pay and Conditions Order
Whether the statutory scheme prevailed over the collective agreement on strike deductions
What deduction was lawful where an employee breached contract by striking
linked_authorities: Miles v Wakefield Metropolitan District Council [1987] ICR 368
Sim v Rotherham Metropolitan Borough Council [1986] ICR 897
Marley v Forward Trust Group Ltd [1996] ICR 891

confidence.notes: Incorporation, statutory interaction, and declaration outcome are explicit. Source metadata lists House of Lords judges from cited authorities rather than the trial judge.

notes: Johnson v Unisys limits recovery of unfair dismissal compensation via wrongful dismissal; appeal reasoning is comprehensive.

enrichment.short_title: Wrongful dismissal damages and loss of unfair dismissal rights
key_facts: Sally Harper was summarily dismissed on 2 March 2001, 33 days before completing one year's continuous employment needed for unfair dismissal protection.
Her contract provided three months' notice but statutory notice was seven days; the effective date of termination was 9 March 2001 under section 97(2).
The employment tribunal awarded notice pay plus damages for loss of the opportunity to claim unfair dismissal, capped at £25,000.
The EAT reduced the award to £9,514.04 in notice pay alone.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from the Employment Appeal Tribunal on whether wrongful dismissal damages may include compensation for loss of statutory unfair dismissal rights.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; an employee cannot recover, as damages for wrongful dismissal, loss flowing from being deprived of the chance to acquire unfair dismissal rights where Parliament has limited the effective date of termination to statutory notice.
enrichment.ratio: Following Johnson v Unisys, courts must not use wrongful dismissal damages to circumvent the statutory unfair dismissal scheme; section 97 postpones the EDT only by reference to statutory minimum notice, not contractual notice, and Parliament deliberately chose not to extend it to contractual notice periods.
legal_issues: Whether damages for wrongful dismissal may include loss of a chance to claim unfair dismissal
Construction of the effective date of termination under section 97 ERA 1996
Whether Brindle v Smith supports recovery via wrongful dismissal
Impact of Johnson v Unisys on loss-of-chance claims in employment contracts
linked_authorities: Johnson v Unisys Ltd [2001] UKHL 13; [2003] 1 AC 518
Brindle v H W Smith (Cabinets) Ltd [1972] IRLR 125
Raspin v United News Shops Ltd [1999] IRLR 9
Robert Cort & Son Ltd v Charman [1981] IRLR 437

confidence.notes: Statutory scheme, EAT reasoning, and Court of Appeal dismissal are fully articulated.

notes: Prison enhanced IEP refusal for denying SOTP attendance; Potter followed and claim refused.

enrichment.short_title: Prison enhanced status refused for SOTP non-attendance
key_facts: A former GP imprisoned for indecent assault sought enhanced status under the Incentives and Earned Privileges scheme.
He remained in denial of the sexual nature of his offences and could not attend a sex offenders treatment programme.
Sentence planning required SOTP completion; the governor refused enhanced status on that ground alone.
He had met eight of nine IEP criteria but failed sentence-plan compliance because of SOTP ineligibility.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of a governor's refusal to grant enhanced prison privileges.
enrichment.outcome: Claim refused; failure to attend an SOTP due to denial of guilt was a sufficient and lawful bar to enhanced IEP status.
enrichment.ratio: Following R (Potter) v SSHD, prison authorities may treat refusal to attend an SOTP as fatal to an application for enhanced status where sentence planning requires programme completion; the Oyston principle on denial of guilt does not apply in this privileges context.
legal_issues: Whether denial of guilt and SOTP non-attendance could bar enhanced IEP status
Application of the Oyston principle to prison privileges
Whether the governor failed to balance other favourable factors
Relevance of CCRC applications and appeal-related IEP policies

notes: Joint enterprise murder directions flawed on withdrawal; Ryan and Toussaint convictions unsafe, O'Flaherty dismissed.

enrichment.short_title: Joint enterprise murder: withdrawal and causation directions
key_facts: Marcus Hall died after street violence outside a Luton nightclub involving rival groups from Peckham and local men.
O'Flaherty, Ryan, and Toussaint were convicted of murder after using a cricket bat, bottle, and claw hammer in Flowers Way.
Fatal stab wounds were likely inflicted in Park Street West; Ryan and Toussaint did not enter that street.
Medical evidence was divided on whether head injuries in Flowers Way contributed significantly to death.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeals against murder and violent disorder convictions following a Crown Court trial.
enrichment.outcome: Appeals of Ryan and Toussaint allowed and convictions quashed as unsafe; O'Flaherty's appeal dismissed.
enrichment.ratio: Even where violence is one continuing incident, the jury must be satisfied fatal injuries were inflicted while the defendant remained within the joint enterprise; Ryan and Toussaint's cases should have been withdrawn, and the one-or-two-events framework wrongly diverted the jury from withdrawal directions required by Mitchell and King.
legal_issues: Whether there was a case to answer for Ryan and Toussaint
Adequacy of directions on one continuing event versus two separate events
Withdrawal or disengagement from spontaneous joint enterprise
Foresight of knife use under Powell and English and Uddin
linked_authorities: R v Powell; R v English [1999] 1 AC 1
R v Uddin [1999] 1 Cr App R 319
R v Mitchell and King (1998) 163 JP 75
R v Grundy (1989) 89 Cr App R 333
R v Whitehouse (1941) 4 WWR 112

notes: Section 459 petition struck out as vexatious; director-notice point and accounting allegations rejected.

enrichment.short_title: Section 459 petition struck out over Oasis management dispute
key_facts: Anthony Branch, a leaseholder member of The Oasis (Poole) Management Ltd, petitioned under section 459 alleging invalid director appointments and financial misconduct.
The company manages a 66-flat residential complex; four director-respondents and the managing agent Owens & Porter were named.
Branch argued AGM notices had to name director candidates; the court held that was wrong in law under the articles and Table A.
Bitter disputes included allegations of fraudulent accounts, improper fund custody, and defamation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application to strike out or dismiss a section 459 unfair prejudice petition under CPR Parts 3.4 and 24.
enrichment.outcome: Petition struck out under CPR Part 3.4 as wholly misconceived and vexatious; receiver appointment application dismissed.
enrichment.ratio: Notice of general meetings need not contain names of proposed directors where articles follow Table A without regulation 77; the petitioner's substantive allegations of invalid appointments, fraudulent accounts, and unfair prejudice lacked any sustainable legal or factual basis.
legal_issues: Whether AGM notices must name candidates for director appointment
Whether director appointments in 2002 and 2003 were invalid
Whether company accounts and budgets were fraudulent or misleading
Whether section 459 relief was available for defamation and managing-agent disputes
linked_authorities: Choppington Collieries Ltd v Johnson [1944] 1 All ER 762
Betts & Co Ltd v Macnaghten [1910] 1 Ch 430

confidence.notes: Strike-out outcome and Table A construction are thoroughly reasoned. Petition contains many rejected allegations.

notes: Parent company guarantee enforced against Holdings; Mannai construction and CEO actual authority findings clear.

enrichment.short_title: Vodafone parent company guarantee enforced against GNT Holdings

statutes_considered.title: Late Payment of Commercial Debts (Interest) Act 1998

key_facts: GNTUK owed Vodafone Ltd £495,419.61 for mobile connections supplied in 2001 and went into creditors' voluntary liquidation in 2003.
Nicholas Barter signed a parent company guarantee on Holdings headed paper as a condition of further supply of 56 SIM cards.
The guarantee was addressed to Vodafone Connect and referred to VUKL, though all trading was with Vodafone Ltd.
Holdings denied authority and argued the guarantee was ineffective for misdescription and lack of consideration.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial of claim on parent company guarantee and alternative breach of warranty of authority against the signing director.
enrichment.outcome: Judgment for Vodafone against Holdings for £495,419.61 plus interest; claim against Mr Barter dismissed as he had actual authority.
enrichment.ratio: Applying Mannai and Investors Compensation Scheme principles, the guarantee must be construed as securing GNTUK's liabilities to Vodafone Ltd despite drafting errors; Mr Barter signed with actual authority after Mr Malkus as CEO approved the guarantee on 2 November 2001.
legal_issues: Whether the guarantee was enforceable despite addressing the wrong Vodafone entity
Whether stated consideration failed because VUKL did not contract with GNTUK
Whether Mr Barter had actual, implied, or ostensible authority
Whether Mr Barter was liable for breach of warranty of authority if unauthorised

notes: Section 42 civil proceedings order against habitual vexatious litigant; extensive litigation history reviewed.

enrichment.short_title: Civil proceedings order against vexatious litigant Lawal
key_facts: Mr Lawal brought at least 15 sets of proceedings since 1996 against former employers, Chesterfield Borough Council, and public bodies.
Many claims involved race discrimination, debt recovery counterclaims, committal applications, and attempts to relitigate decided matters.
A £36.96 council debt claim generated numerous abusive applications over several years.
Two employment cases had partial success but the overall pattern was of hopeless, repetitive litigation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application by the Attorney General under section 42 of the Supreme Court Act 1981 for a civil proceedings order.
enrichment.outcome: Civil proceedings order made without limit of time; Mr Lawal may not institute or continue civil proceedings without High Court leave.
enrichment.ratio: Mr Lawal habitually and persistently instituted vexatious civil proceedings without reasonable ground; proceedings lacked legal basis, caused disproportionate harassment and expense, and abused court process within the meaning of Attorney General v Barker.
legal_issues: Whether section 42 conditions for a civil proceedings order were satisfied
Whether the Employment Tribunal is an inferior court for section 42 purposes
Whether two partially successful claims outweighed the vexatious litigation history
Appropriate scope and duration of the order
linked_authorities: Attorney General v Barker [2000] FLR 759

notes: Section 14A Limitation Act appeal allowed on accountants negligence date-of-knowledge issue; constructive notice remitted.

enrichment.short_title: Section 14A limitation date of knowledge in accountants negligence
key_facts: Mr Haward and related entities sued accountants Fawcetts for negligence over the 1994 acquisition of and investment in Haward Agriculture Ltd.
Fawcetts pleaded limitation in respect of losses before 6 December 1995; the claimants relied on section 14A and alleged knowledge only from 17 December 1999.
A preliminary issue trial held most of the claim time-barred, debarring pre-December 1995 damages.
The claim against solicitors Whiteheads was resolved separately with judgment entered for the claimants.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a preliminary issue trial on section 14A Limitation Act 1980 date of knowledge.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; preliminary issue determined in favour of the claimants on actual knowledge, but constructive notice under section 14A(10) was not investigated and could not be resolved on appeal.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 14A(8)(a) the claimant must have knowledge of the act or omission causally relevant to the pleaded negligence, not merely that damage was caused by the defendant; the judge erred in treating the causal connection as obvious before May 1999 when the claimants learned the underlying causes of continuing losses.
legal_issues: Construction of section 14A(5)-(9) date of knowledge provisions
What constitutes knowledge of acts or omissions causally relevant to negligence
Whether the judge erred in finding knowledge before 6 December 1998
Whether constructive notice under section 14A(10) could be decided without findings at first instance
linked_authorities: Hallam-Eames v Merrett Syndicates Ltd [2000] Lloyd's Rep IR 153
Dobbie v Medway Health Authority [2001] Lloyd's Rep PN 183
Broadley v De Padua [1996] 4 All ER 774
Oakes v Hopcroft [2002] EWCA Civ 792

notes: Green Belt gypsy site planning appeal challenge dismissed; inspector's education and health balancing upheld.

enrichment.short_title: Green Belt gypsy caravan site planning appeal challenge
key_facts: Mrs Williams sought retrospective planning permission for a gypsy caravan site and access road at The Meadows, Pucklechurch, in the Bristol/Bath Green Belt.
The local authority refused permission and an inspector dismissed her appeal, finding harm outweighed very special circumstances.
There was unmet need for settled gypsy accommodation locally and no locational or criteria-based council sites in adopted plans.
The family faced possible roadside accommodation with disruption to children's schooling and long-term medical care.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Section 288 challenge to an inspector's dismissal of a planning appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Challenge refused; inspector lawfully concluded very special circumstances did not outweigh Green Belt and amenity harm and Article 8 interference was proportionate.
enrichment.ratio: The inspector did not err in treating education and health disruption as not very special circumstances; his references to moves in the wider community did not negate his recognition that roadside accommodation was a real possibility, and quashing of Policy 37 did not undermine a decision that did not rely on it.
legal_issues: Whether the inspector failed to assess impact of itinerant life on education and health
Whether very special circumstances existed to justify Green Belt development
Whether Article 8 ECHR was violated by dismissal of the appeal
Whether reliance on subsequently quashed Policy 37 invalidated the decision
linked_authorities: Butler v Bath and North East Somerset District Council [2003] EWCA Civ 1614

confidence.notes: Inspector's reasoning, challenge grounds, and refusal of section 288 application are clearly explained.

notes: SEND Tribunal decision quashed for failing to specify out-of-hours educational provision in statement.

enrichment.short_title: SEN statement defective for out-of-hours provision
key_facts: HW, a child with spastic quadriplegic cerebral palsy and significant learning difficulties, appealed against his Statement of Special Educational Needs.
He attended residential St Mary's school receiving intensive education outside normal school hours; parents sought continuation of that provision.
Bedfordshire LEA proposed Ridgeway day school at lower cost, arguing social services could provide out-of-hours care.
The SEND Tribunal chose Ridgeway but did not address how out-of-hours educational needs in Part 2 would be met.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Statutory appeal under section 326 of the Education Act 1996 against a SEND Tribunal decision.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; tribunal decision quashed and remitted to a fresh tribunal.
enrichment.ratio: A statement must specify provision to meet identified needs; where the tribunal rejected residential schooling but accepted out-of-hours provision was required, it failed to determine how that need would be met and a vague reference to a package of care was insufficient.
legal_issues: Whether the statement adequately specified provision for out-of-hours educational needs
Whether social services provision could substitute for educational provision in the statement
Whether the tribunal properly compared costs under section 9
Whether unreasonable public expenditure analysis was flawed without quantified social services costs

confidence.notes: Defect in the tribunal decision and remittal order are clearly explained on the agreed facts.
